blocks.text: A whole family of problems asks about **contiguous runs** of an array — the largest sum of any five consecutive numbers, the longest stretch without a repeat, the shortest run adding up to at least some target.

The brute force generates every possible run and evaluates it. There are roughly N²/2 of them, and evaluating each costs up to N, so you land at **O(N³)** — hopeless. The sliding window pattern gets most of these to **O(N)**.
Look at two neighbouring windows of size 3 in `[4, 2, 7, 1, 9]`:

blocks.code:
window A:  [4, 2, 7]      sum 13
window B:     [2, 7, 1]   sum 10

blocks.text: They share `2` and `7`. Recomputing the sum from scratch re-adds both. For a window of size k you redo k − 1 additions every single step — and that redundancy is the entire cost.
Do not rebuild the window. **Update** it. Moving one step right means exactly one value leaves and one value enters:

blocks.alt: A window of three cells sliding one step, losing the leftmost value and gaining a new right one
blocks.caption: Sliding one step: subtract what leaves, add what enters

blocks.code:
new sum  =  old sum  -  value leaving  +  value entering
     10  =        13  -             4  +             1

blocks.text: Two operations per step, regardless of how wide the window is. N steps, constant work each: **O(N)**.
Which one you need depends on whether the width is given to you:

items: **Fixed size** — the problem names the width ("every subarray of size k"). Both edges move together in lockstep.
**Variable size** — the problem names a *condition* ("the longest run with no repeats"). The right edge grows the window; the left edge shrinks it when the condition breaks.

blocks.text: Sliding window applies when all of these hold:

items: The answer is about a **contiguous** run — elements next to each other, not a scattered selection.
You want a maximum, minimum, or count over those runs.
A window's value can be **updated incrementally** rather than recomputed.

blocks.text: That last point is the real test. If adding or removing one element cannot cheaply update your running answer, the window will not save you anything.
And note the family resemblance: `left` and `right` are two pointers that only move forward. This chapter is the two pointer pattern, pointed in a different direction.
